programs.subtitle: Apple II, 1989

programs.introduction:
In the summer of 1985, Jordan Mechner sat down at his Apple II computer in his parents' home in Chappaqua, New York, with a vision that would redefine the boundaries of video games. Fresh off the success of his first game, 'Karateka,' Mechner was determined to create something more ambitious — a game that would feel like a movie, blending fluid animation, gripping storytelling, and precise gameplay. Over the next four years, he would work alone, crafting every line of code in 6502 assembly, pushing the Apple II hardware to its absolute limits. By the time 'Prince of Persia' was released in 1989, it had become a masterpiece of ingenuity, a game that invented the cinematic platformer genre and set new standards for animation and immersion.

The computing world of the mid-1980s was a landscape of constraints. The Apple II, introduced in 1977, was still a popular platform, but its hardware was aging. With just 128K of RAM and a 1 MHz 6502 processor, developers faced tight memory limits and slow processing speeds. Mechner had to use bank-switched memory — juggling between auxiliary and main memory, as well as the language card's two banks — to fit his game into the available space. Every decision was shaped by these constraints: the sound engine operated through a single speaker, the animation system relied on clever memory management, and the physics engine had to calculate gravity and momentum within razor-thin computational margins. Yet, Mechner saw these limitations not as obstacles but as challenges to overcome.

Mechner's approach to animation was groundbreaking. Inspired by the fluid movements of characters in classic films like 'Raiders of the Lost Ark,' he wanted the prince to move with lifelike grace. To achieve this, he filmed his younger brother David performing jumps, climbs, and sword fights, then traced each frame by hand — a technique known as rotoscoping. This painstaking process resulted in animation that felt revolutionary for the time, with the prince's movements flowing naturally in a way that no other game had achieved. Mechner also designed the game's collision detection and physics engine to complement this realism, ensuring that every jump, fall, and swing felt precise and believable.

The source code itself reveals the depth of Mechner's craftsmanship. Files like SOUND.S showcase the minimalist sound engine, where twenty distinct sounds were crafted for a single speaker without compromising the game's atmosphere. BOOT.S contains the two-stage disk boot loader, which checks for the required 128K of memory before initializing the game. SEQTABLE.S manages the animation state machine, meticulously programmed to handle every rotoscoped movement. CTRL.S handles player input, while MOVER.S calculates gravity and momentum, and COLL.S detects collisions between the prince and the dungeon's treacherous environment. Together, these files form the backbone of a game that feels seamless and cinematic, even on hardware that was considered outdated by 1989.

When 'Prince of Persia' was released, it was met with critical acclaim, and its influence was immediate. The game introduced the concept of cinematic platformers, inspiring countless imitators and successors. Its fluid animation and immersive gameplay raised the bar for what video games could achieve, influencing not just platformers but the broader gaming industry. Decades later, the game remains iconic, with its source code recovered in 2012 from 22-year-old floppy disks, allowing a new generation to appreciate the brilliance of Mechner's work. Today, 'Prince of Persia' stands as a testament to the power of creativity and determination, proving that even the most constrained hardware can produce timeless artistry.

programs.introduction:
In the summer of 1981, a seismic shift in personal computing was quietly underway in Bellevue, Washington. Tim Paterson, a 25-year-old programmer at Seattle Computer Products, had just completed a remarkable feat: writing an operating system in only six weeks. That system, originally called 86-DOS, was born out of necessity. SCP needed software to run on its Intel 8086-based computer kits, and Paterson, armed with a copy of Digital Research's CP/M manual and a deep understanding of assembly language, set out to create it. Little did he know, his work would soon become the foundation for MS-DOS, the operating system that would define the PC era.

The computing world of 1981 was a fragmented landscape. The IBM PC, launched on August 12 of that year, was a bold gamble by the corporate giant to enter the personal computer market. Its hardware featured the Intel 8088 processor, 64 KB of RAM, and a 5.25-inch floppy drive, all for a base price of $1,565. But IBM needed software to make its machine useful, and CP/M, the dominant OS of the time, was unavailable due to licensing issues. Microsoft, then a small company led by Bill Gates and Paul Allen, seized the opportunity. Gates negotiated to acquire 86-DOS from SCP for $25,000, hired Paterson, and adapted the system into PC DOS 1.0 for IBM. Crucially, Microsoft retained the rights to license MS-DOS to other manufacturers, a decision that would prove transformative.

Tim Paterson's background as a self-taught programmer and hardware enthusiast shaped his approach to 86-DOS. He designed the system to be simple and fast, leveraging the 8086 assembly language to maximize performance on the limited hardware of the time. The early versions of MS-DOS were minimalist, offering basic file management and program execution. Paterson later reflected, "I never imagined it would become the standard for an entire industry." By 1983, MS-DOS had evolved into version 2.0, a near-complete rewrite inspired by Unix and XENIX. This update introduced revolutionary features like subdirectories, file handles, and device drivers, laying the groundwork for modern operating systems.

The licensing strategy that Microsoft pursued was as pivotal as the software itself. Within a year of the IBM PC's launch, MS-DOS had been licensed to over 70 manufacturers of IBM-compatible machines. This created an ecosystem of PC clones that fueled the rapid growth of personal computing in the 1980s. MS-DOS became synonymous with the PC, and its influence extended far beyond its original design. The FAT filesystem, introduced in MS-DOS, remained a standard for decades, even surviving into modern flash drives and SD cards.

The legacy of MS-DOS is both technical and cultural. It reshaped the software industry, establishing Microsoft as a dominant force and setting the stage for the Windows operating system. Its source code, released to the Computer History Museum in 2014 under an MIT license, offers a glimpse into the ingenuity and constraints of early computing. From the terse assembly comments in MSDOS.ASM to the iconic "Abort, Retry, Ignore?" message in COMMAND.ASM, MS-DOS is a testament to how a small team, working under tight deadlines, can change the world. Today, its influence persists in the DNA of modern operating systems, a reminder of the era when the PC revolution began.

programs.introduction:
In the summer of 1977, two young programmers, Bill Gates and Paul Allen, sat down to tackle an ambitious challenge that would help define the future of computing. The personal computer revolution was just beginning, and the newly released MOS Technology 6502 microprocessor offered an affordable and powerful foundation for small-scale machines. Gates and Allen, co-founders of Microsoft, were already gaining recognition for their earlier work on BASIC for the Altair 8800, but now they faced a new frontier: adapting their programming language to the 6502, a chip that would soon power iconic machines like the Apple II. The stakes were high, and the constraints were daunting. They had to create a fully functional BASIC interpreter that could fit into just a few kilobytes of memory.

The computing world of 1977 was a landscape of innovation and limitation. Microprocessors like the 6502 were revolutionizing hardware design, offering performance at a fraction of the cost of earlier systems. Yet, memory was scarce and expensive—early personal computers often shipped with as little as 4 KB of RAM. Every byte mattered, and programming in assembly language was not just a choice but a necessity. The 6502 assembly language was both powerful and unforgiving, requiring programmers to think in terms of registers, memory addresses, and cycles. Gates and Allen, already seasoned in the art of squeezing functionality into tight spaces, approached the task with a mix of technical rigor and entrepreneurial urgency.

Bill Gates, a Harvard dropout with a penchant for optimization, and Paul Allen, a self-taught programmer with a deep understanding of hardware, were perfectly suited to the task. Their earlier success with Altair BASIC had proven their ability to deliver compact, efficient code, but the 6502 posed new challenges. The chip’s architecture was different from the Intel 8080 they had worked with before, requiring a complete rewrite of their interpreter. Gates reportedly spent weeks poring over the 6502’s instruction set, while Allen focused on debugging and testing the code on prototype hardware. “We had to make every instruction count,” Gates later recalled, emphasizing the painstaking effort to fit the program into the available memory.

The result of their work was Microsoft BASIC for the 6502, a triumph of engineering and ingenuity. The interpreter provided a full suite of BASIC commands, enabling users to write and execute programs on early personal computers. It was fast, efficient, and remarkably compact, fitting comfortably within the limited memory of machines like the Apple II. This achievement was not just a technical milestone; it was a commercial breakthrough. Microsoft licensed the software to multiple manufacturers, establishing itself as a key player in the burgeoning personal computer industry. The Apple II, powered in part by Microsoft BASIC, became one of the most successful early PCs, selling millions of units and cementing BASIC as the programming language of choice for hobbyists and professionals alike.

Microsoft BASIC for the 6502 left an indelible mark on computing history. It demonstrated that software could be as transformative as hardware, enabling ordinary people to harness the power of computers for education, business, and creativity. The program’s influence extended far beyond the 1970s, laying the groundwork for Microsoft’s rise as a software giant and inspiring generations of programmers to explore the possibilities of personal computing. Today, the source code for Microsoft BASIC stands as a testament to the ingenuity and determination of its creators, a snapshot of a pivotal moment when two visionaries helped shape the digital age.

programs.introduction:
In the spring of 1992, inside a modest office in Madison, Wisconsin, three young programmers—John Carmack, John Romero, and Tom Hall—were on the verge of revolutionizing the gaming industry. The team at id Software was small but fiercely ambitious, driven by a shared vision of creating fast-paced, immersive experiences that had never been seen before. Their latest project, Wolfenstein 3D, was born out of a desire to push the boundaries of what personal computers could achieve. The stakes were high: MS-DOS was the dominant platform, but its limitations were daunting. Memory was scarce, graphics capabilities were primitive, and performance was constrained by the modest power of Intel’s 386 processors. Yet, these constraints only fueled their ingenuity.

The computing world of 1992 was a landscape of compromise. PCs were equipped with processors running at clock speeds of 25 to 33 MHz, and most machines had no more than 4 MB of RAM. Graphics cards were rudimentary, offering resolutions that paled in comparison to today’s standards. The prevailing wisdom was that smooth scrolling and real-time 3D environments were beyond the reach of consumer hardware. But John Carmack, the technical wizard of id Software, refused to accept those limitations. Drawing on his deep understanding of assembly language and low-level programming, Carmack developed a groundbreaking raycasting engine that simulated 3D environments with remarkable efficiency. “It’s not about what the hardware can do,” he once said, “it’s about what you can make it do.”

Tom Hall, the creative force behind the project, infused Wolfenstein 3D with a sense of atmosphere and narrative. Inspired by the 1981 stealth-action game Castle Wolfenstein, Hall envisioned a fast-paced shooter set in a Nazi stronghold, where players could experience the thrill of infiltration and combat. Meanwhile, John Romero, the team’s design virtuoso, focused on crafting gameplay that was intuitive yet exhilarating. Romero’s philosophy was simple: “Make it fun, make it fast, and make it unforgettable.” Together, the trio made key decisions that defined the game’s identity, from its responsive controls to its iconic sound effects, brought to life by the ID_SD.C sound driver code.

Wolfenstein 3D’s source code was a masterclass in optimization. Files like C0.ASM showcased Carmack’s ability to squeeze every ounce of performance out of the hardware, while ID_CA.C introduced innovative caching techniques that allowed the game to handle large levels within tight memory constraints. The rendering code in WL_DRAW.C was a marvel, enabling players to navigate labyrinthine corridors with fluid motion. Every subsystem was meticulously crafted, from the WL_MENU.C interface to the WL_PLAY.C gameplay logic, ensuring a seamless experience that felt ahead of its time.

The impact of Wolfenstein 3D was immediate and profound. Upon its release, the game was hailed as a technical and creative triumph, selling over 200,000 copies in its first year and earning id Software a place in gaming history. It defined the first-person shooter genre, paving the way for future classics like Doom and Quake. The source code, later released as open source, became a treasure trove for aspiring developers, offering insights into the techniques that powered one of gaming’s most influential titles. Even today, echoes of Wolfenstein 3D’s innovations can be found in modern game engines and design philosophies, a testament to the enduring legacy of Carmack, Romero, and Hall’s groundbreaking work.

programs.introduction:
It was December 10, 1993, and in a small office in Mesquite, Texas, the team at id Software was about to unleash a revolution. John Carmack, John Romero, Dave Taylor, and their colleagues had spent months pushing the limits of what a personal computer could do, and the culmination of their efforts was DOOM—a game that would redefine the industry. Carmack, the quiet programming prodigy, had been working tirelessly to perfect the engine, while Romero, the charismatic designer, infused the game with his signature flair for fast-paced, visceral action. Taylor contributed his expertise in optimizing the game for the hardware of the day, ensuring it could run smoothly on the modest PCs of the early 1990s. Together, they were about to change gaming forever.

The computing world of 1993 was a landscape of constraints and ingenuity. Consumer PCs like the Intel 386 and 486 were the norm, with clock speeds measured in megahertz and memory often capped at 4 to 8 megabytes. Graphics cards were rudimentary, offering limited acceleration, and sound cards like the Sound Blaster were just beginning to gain widespread adoption. Yet, id Software saw potential in this hardware. Carmack's programming genius allowed DOOM to simulate immersive 3D environments on machines that were never designed for such feats. Using techniques like binary space partitioning (BSP) for efficient rendering and a modular architecture to manage assets, the team crafted a game that felt years ahead of its time.

The development of DOOM was driven by a mix of technical ambition and creative vision. Carmack famously stated, "Story in a game is like a story in a porn movie. It's expected to be there, but it's not that important." His focus was on the engine—the foundation that made DOOM's fast-paced gameplay and multiplayer networking possible. Romero, on the other hand, was obsessed with creating an experience that would thrill players, designing levels that were as memorable as they were challenging. Taylor worked to ensure the game was accessible, optimizing it for systems without cutting corners on performance. The team's synergy was palpable, and their shared belief in pushing boundaries was evident in every line of code.

When DOOM was released, it was nothing short of a phenomenon. Players marveled at its fluid movement, eerie sound design, and groundbreaking multiplayer deathmatches. The game's shareware model allowed millions to experience the first episode for free, creating an instant fanbase and setting a precedent for distribution in the industry. The source code, later released in 1997, became a treasure trove for developers and enthusiasts, offering insights into techniques that would influence game design for decades. From its rendering pipeline to its memory management, DOOM's architecture showcased a level of ingenuity that inspired countless imitators and successors.

DOOM didn't just change gaming; it changed culture. It popularized the first-person shooter genre, introduced multiplayer gaming to a wider audience, and demonstrated the potential of PCs as gaming platforms. Its influence is still felt today, with modern engines tracing their lineage back to the innovations Carmack and his team pioneered. The game's source code remains a touchstone for programmers, a testament to what can be achieved when creativity meets technical mastery. For id Software, DOOM was more than a game—it was a legacy, one that continues to shape the digital world.
